Testify
TES-tih-fy
v.
From Latin testificari, “to bear witness,” from testis (witness) + facere (to make). Renders the Greek martureō, “to bear witness,” and diamarturomai, “to bear thorough witness, charge solemnly”; and the Hebrew ‘ūd, “to bear witness, testify.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To testify is to bear witness—to declare under solemn responsibility what one has seen, heard, or received, with one’s name attached to the testimony and one’s person standing behind it. In Scripture, the verb is courtroom-shaped: a witness testifies to a fact, and the truth or falsity of his testimony is a matter of judgment, with severe penalties for false witness. The chief use of the word is christological and apostolic. The Father testifies to the Son: this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. The Spirit testifies of Christ: he shall testify of me. The Scriptures testify of Christ: they are they which testify of me. The apostles are appointed as Christ’s witnesses: ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. Their testimony is the founding deposit of Christian truth—the historical witness to the life, death, resurrection, and lordship of Jesus Christ, codified in the New Testament and proclaimed in the church’s mission. The ongoing testimony of the church is derivative of and bound to this apostolic deposit: every believer is to be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you, and the Spirit of God bears witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God. Testimony in the New Testament therefore has both an objective face (the apostolic witness to historical fact, summarized in the gospel) and a personal face (the believer’s own life and word standing behind the gospel he confesses). Both are essential; neither is the whole; and both together are what Christ means when He sends His church into the world as witnesses unto Him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TESTIFY as to make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact; to bear witness; to declare a fact or facts, especially in a court of justice; in scripture, to declare or publish solemnly.

expand to see more

TESTIFY, v.i. — To make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact; to give testimony for the purpose of communicating to others a knowledge of something not known to them. In a court of justice, to make a solemn declaration under oath, for the purpose of establishing or making proof of some fact to a court.

TESTIFY, v.t. — 1. To bear witness to; to support the truth of by testimony. 2. To affirm or declare solemnly for the purpose of establishing a fact (1 Cor 15:15). 3. In scripture, to publish and declare freely (Acts 20:21).

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 1:8 — "But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth."

John 15:26 — "But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me."

John 5:39 — "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me."

1 Peter 3:15 — "...be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Testimony is corrupted by the self-referential turn of the age, which reduces it from witness-to-Christ to autobiography-about-me, and by the affective storytelling register that prizes emotional resonance over the propositional content of what is testified.

expand to see more

The modern evangelical ‘testimony’ has drifted from its New Testament moorings. In Scripture, to testify is to bear witness to Christ—to His person, His work, His resurrection, His lordship; the witness’s own story is the occasion, not the substance, of the testimony. In much contemporary use, the proportion has been inverted: the autobiography becomes the substance and Christ becomes the occasion, the testimony is judged by how moving the personal narrative is rather than by how clearly the gospel is set forth, and a generation rises that has heard many testimonies and very little explicit witness to who Christ is and what He has done. Recover the apostolic shape: testify to Him; tell your story only so far as it serves to make Him plain.

Testimony is also corrupted by the affective storytelling register that prizes emotional resonance over the propositional content of what is testified. The witness in the New Testament is courtroom-shaped: he says what is so. His testimony stands or falls by whether it is true. The believer’s answer to the man who asks a reason of the hope must include actual reasons—the historical fact of the resurrection, the propositions of the gospel, the doctrines that constitute the hope—and not only the texture of the believer’s experience. Recover both ends: the personal face (the believer’s life and word standing behind what he confesses) and the objective face (the apostolic content of the gospel itself, faithfully testified). The faithful witness is both: a real person bearing a real message about a real Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek martureō (to bear witness) and diamarturomai (to bear thorough witness, charge solemnly); Hebrew ‘ūd (to bear witness)—the courtroom-shaped declaration of fact under solemn responsibility.

expand to see more

Greek martureō (G3140) — to bear witness, testify; the root behind martyr, the witness who seals his testimony with his blood.

Greek diamarturomai (G1263) — to bear thorough witness, charge solemnly—Paul’s frequent word for solemn testimony.

Greek marturia (G3141) — the noun: witness, testimony.

Hebrew ‘ūd (H5749) — to bear witness, testify, charge solemnly.

Usage

"Testifying is courtroom-shaped: the witness says what is so, with his name attached and his person standing behind it."

"The apostolic testimony to Christ’s resurrection is the founding deposit of Christian truth—all subsequent witness is derivative of it and bound to it."

"The modern testimony has often inverted the proportion: the autobiography becomes the substance and Christ becomes the occasion; the apostolic shape must be recovered."
